prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, a new class of atomic clock that brought frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B022 alone as my preferred configuration. The first round did not weaken the scientific case; it sharpened what that case is. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is a genuine idea about atomic structure: it makes the differential light shift of the clock transition vanish while thousands of atoms are held Doppler- and recoil-free. Ye's group then showed what the idea could do, with record systematic uncertainty, long coherence, the Fermi-degenerate many-body clock and the frequency transfer that lets independent clocks be compared. That comparison step matters most for maturity. The 10^-18 level has been reproduced and confirmed across several laboratories, so it rests on measurement and not on interpretation. The credit is two people whose roles are separable and complementary, a better fit to the three-name limit than any other part on the table. I am no longer inclined to argue that the redefinition of the second supports the timing, since Pearce and Kroll are right that this is a metrological decision and not scientific verification. The case rests on the demonstrated capability and on a citation that names the lattice clock explicitly, so that it reads as a distinct step beyond the combs of 2005 and the single-ion control of 2012.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against remains overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which Mehlig stated forcefully, together with the point that the largest consequences for fundamental physics, such as constants, dark-matter searches and a redefined second, are so far bounds and prospects and not discoveries. Danielsson and Eriksson are right on this and I do not want to overstate it: the geodesy and comparison results are demonstrated, but the new-physics reach is still prospective. Credit is also incomplete, since Lemonde, Derevianko, the JILA and RIKEN teams around the two laureates, and the NIST ion-clock groups lie outside the names. Finally, B028 has the broadest ballot support in the room, and I cannot dismiss that, though breadth of support is not a scientific argument and I do not weigh it as one.

responses.point: Danielsson regards B022 as a strong instrument prize whose fundamental-physics consequences are mostly prospective, so he would pair it with a discovery in the strict sense, B002, and he would exclude the Galactic-plane result from any IceCube citation.
responses.response: I accept the factual point that constants and dark-matter searches have so far produced bounds, and I have dropped that as a lead argument. What the clock demonstrates is a measurement capability that did not exist before, 10^-18 comparisons that resolve gravitational redshift over centimetres, and that is a demonstrated result and not a promise. Where I differ is on the remedy. The prize has honoured instruments and measurements that opened a regime, and I do not think B022 needs a partner to be complete. Pairing it with B002 would still be driven by two overlapping lists of supporters and not by a shared scientific argument, and the reservations you and Pearce both voice about one name for a collaboration of hundreds are not answered by the chair's summary. I would reconsider only if the external experts clearly settle the AMANDA to IceCube credit, and even then I would see two unrelated achievements as a choice, not a necessity.

responses.point: Mehlig maintains that B022 is mostly a story of ever-improving accuracy, narrower in novelty than B028, which opened a new class of many-body phenomena, although he grants the attribution is cleaner and defers partly to Kroll and me on significance.
responses.response: I take the deference seriously and want to earn it, not trade on it. My answer to improving accuracy is that the lattice clock is not a better version of an existing clock. Earlier optical clocks were limited either by one ion's low signal-to-noise or by Doppler and recoil shifts in neutral atoms, and the magic-wavelength lattice removes that trade-off by an argument from the atomic level structure. The many-body clock then turns the large atom number from a nuisance into the resource. That is a conceptual step, though it is expressed in a measurement. I agree that B028 opened a larger new field, and if the committee's criterion were breadth of follow-on physics it would win. But you also said you would not strongly object to B022, and your ranking of it seventh rested on novelty, which I have tried to address directly, not on any doubt about the result.

responses.point: Eriksson says the B022 case rests on a precision result whose largest consequences are still prospective, and he explicitly asks Kroll and me whether the fundamental-physics reach is already demonstrated.
responses.response: You asked directly, so here is my assessment as a theorist who works on atomic structure and relativistic effects. The demonstrated part is that clocks at this level resolve relativistic redshift across height differences of centimetres, that independent lattice clocks agree within their uncertainties, and that they place tightened limits on drifts in the fine-structure constant and on certain dark-matter couplings. The prospective part is any positive detection of new physics. That distinction is real and I would keep it out of the citation, which should name the clock and its precision. Your preference for B028 also does not seem to me to follow from this point, since B028's headline phase is not explained either. In both cases I think the prize should honour the reproducible discovery and avoid claiming the mechanism, and I would hold B022 to that same standard.

responses.point: Olsson argues that the open mechanism in B028 is not a reason to wait, that the discovery rests on reproducible measurements, and that B028 is a new platform whereas B022 overlaps the 2005 and 2012 frequency-metrology prizes.
responses.response: Your comparison with the fractional quantum Hall effect and topological phases is fair, and I agree that an unresolved pairing mechanism should not by itself rule B028 out, as I said of B022's own prospective reach. My disagreement is narrower. For B028 the committee is choosing a three-name credit that leaves out Cao and the first-author experimental team, and you and Eriksson both concede that the Bistritzer question is unresolved, so the attribution is not yet as defensible as the platform. If the committee does prefer B028, I would support wording it around flat bands and correlated phases and would regard that as a serious outcome, which is why B028 is now my first alternative. On the overlap, the 2005 prize gave the frequency comb and the 2012 prize control of single quantum systems; I do not think either covers a many-atom lattice at 10^-18, and I would insist the citation says so.

responses.point: Kroll supports the two-person B022 allocation but asks that the citation state explicitly that the lattice clock is a distinct step beyond comb-based and single-ion work, and he has disclosed a research stay in Hall's laboratory in Boulder.
responses.response: I agree and have changed my own citation accordingly, naming the optical lattice clock as a new class of clock. I would not treat your Boulder stay as a recusal matter. Katori and Ye are credited for work that postdates it, and you document no collaboration with either, so a note in the record seems sufficient to me. I would also ask that we not lean on your earlier argument that this is a record of accuracy as such. If the committee needs one reason to prefer B022 over a prize in an adjacent area, it should be the capability it opens, and that is the argument I would make to the Academy.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the lattice clock distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which turns on a judgement about novelty that the supplied record cannot settle for me.
Whether the split between Katori's concept and Ye's accuracy and many-body work is fairly captured by two names, with Lemonde and the NIST ion-clock groups outside it.
Whether external experts would settle the AMANDA to IceCube attribution in a way that makes B002 defensible, which would change my view of a two-part prize but not my preference for B022 alone.
Whether B028 is mature enough, which I cannot resolve from outside condensed-matter physics and on which I defer to Eriksson, Olsson and Mehlig.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and with Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato, and training in Lindgren's group. None of these people is credited in any shortlisted part, and no relationship with Katori or Ye is documented. B022 lies close to my own field of atomic structure, and I flag that closeness again for the record, but it is intellectual proximity and not a personal or institutional tie. I do not judge that recusal is required, and I would accept the committee's decision if it disagrees.
